I must thank the entire team at the clinic. A heartfelt thank you to Dr. Sette and Dr. Polito, who have always cared for my cat, Fulmine. Thanks to their professionalism, expertise, and care, he is coping with kidney failure in the best possible way. At every visit, we found helpfulness, clarity, and a great love for animals. A special thank you also goes to Dr. Cervellini, who saved my cat's eye twice in a month for different reasons. His expertise, precision, and dedication made the difference in very difficult times, allowing my cat to recover and maintain his sight. Knowing I can count on such well-trained and attentive professionals gives me great peace of mind. I recommend them to anyone looking for a trusted partner for their pet's well-being.

A top-notch veterinary practice. Dr. Bellucci, Dr. Polito, and the entire team stand out for their superior medical expertise, great professionalism, and rare humanity. Over the years, we have always received solid support, clear explanations, and genuine attention to the well-being of our animals.

Professional, serious and reliable.

My veterinary practice has always been there, they're like family!!!
Excellent staff!!

I took my dog, almost eleven years old, on June 24th for limping and a large swelling in her left hind leg, along with loss of appetite and fatigue. Dr. Bellucci performed a superficial, tactile examination, and prescribed an anti-inflammatory for her joints. After finishing one box, the problem recurred, and over the phone, without an examination, I was advised to continue the treatment. Some improvement occurred, but not completely. I thought it might be her age. I have no veterinary training. Over the weekend of July 19th-20th, I noticed a pronounced abdominal sac and found two ticks, which I successfully removed using alcohol and tweezers. Friends recommended a visit, as the abdominal sac was incompatible with the presence of ticks. On the morning of July 21st, my girlfriend brought the dog to the office for a check-up. She was treated as if she were overly considerate, the ticks were removed correctly, the dog was fine; it was her, Naisha, the dog, who was "a scaredy-cat." A cursory and superficial visit, for which they didn't even want to be paid. I don't know who the doctor was who performed the examination. In the following days, the dog was quite well, with only a slight loss of appetite at times, but it was also very hot. He didn't particularly like kibble, but he enjoyed eating fresh food. On August 9th, the dog was very weak and had a noticeable growth on his back. The Bellucci practice was closed all month. We went to another practice in Corbetta. We were immediately advised to have an X-ray of the affected limb, an ultrasound, blood tests, and cytology of the growths, which also found a smaller one on the left side. The ultrasound revealed a 15 cm diameter growth on the left hind limb, a 10 cm one on the back, and a 3 cm one on the spleen. A cytology of these growths was immediately scheduled. Blood tests arrived that evening and showed moderate anemia. The picture wasn't good, but we had to wait for the cytology results. The next day, August 10th, she's fine, eating and playing. On August 11th, she barely gets up. She has the abdominal sac again, like in July, and she's weak and distraught. We return to the office, this time with an oncologist. They perform an ultrasound of her lungs, which reveals several nodules. The abdominal sac is bruised, clearly a sign of blood loss. A blood test is done, her platelet count is 13, and she needs a transfusion. Her clinical picture is grim; crucially, the dog is riddled with tumors, and we reluctantly decide to put her to sleep to avoid unnecessary suffering. Everything went sour too quickly. In the space of three days. I thought the dog was healthy. Then the cytology results arrive, which are consistent with metastatic soft tissue cancer. Nothing, Nai is no longer alive.

Dear Dr. Bellucci, I'm not a veterinarian, and we rely on professionals to ensure the best care for our beloved animals.
Over the past few days, I've been researching, talking to other doctors, reading, and taking an interest in the situation. Almost certainly, had a correct diagnosis been made in June/July, things wouldn't have changed much, at least for Naisha, but for me, they did. A limp requires more attention at that age, not to mention the severe swelling she had and, above all, an abdominal sac like that, which couldn't have been caused by two ticks. I know this now; you have years of experience. I would have acted differently in many ways, giving her more attention, care, and love than I always have. The diagnosis, which, in hindsight and considering the clinical picture and the patient's age, was quite simple to verify. Everyone told me that at least an X-ray and a blood test should have been done. I trusted them. I trusted a rough and completely wrong diagnosis. Sometimes, for a "client," it's better to spend 100-150 euros and remove all possible doubts. Now Nai is no longer with us, and it's certainly not his fault. When you all return from your wonderful month of vacation, I'll come in person to greet you and shake your hand, hoping for your due apologies.
For being the first time, I had a good first impression: professionalism, organization, availability, and, most importantly, a wonderful approach with the animals.
Went to the doctor, really kind and nice. Comfortable facility and very professional.

I showed up with my dog ​​in critical respiratory distress, crying for help. They locked her in a cage alone, without examining her, while she gasped for breath, and told me to wait in the waiting room. After more than fifteen minutes of waiting and desperate pleas, I was told to take her elsewhere because it wasn't an emergency clinic, and if I couldn't wait, it was best for me to leave, despite the dog dying and my panicked state. A few hours later, I had to put her down, so she wouldn't suffer any more. Total inhumanity.
